analysis.one_liner: Bans tobacco sales to anyone under 21, with photo ID checks for buyers under 30.
analysis.headline: Despite 18 cosponsors from both parties, the bill died in the Senate Commerce Committee without ever receiving a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it illegal nationwide to sell tobacco products, including e-cigarettes, to anyone under 21, and would have required stores to check a photo ID for any buyer under 30. The FDA would enforce the ban with undercover compliance checks, retailer inspections, and penalties for stores that violate it. The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in April 2019 and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Young people who would otherwise start smoking, since about 94% of adult smokers begin before age 21, plus taxpayers who foot the bill for tobacco-related disease and everyone exposed to secondhand smoke. The bill's own findings cite projections that a national age-21 law would, over time, cut smoking rates 12% and prevent 223,000 premature deaths among people born between 2000 and 2019.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Young people, taxpayers, and public health

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits all commercial sales of tobacco products — including e-cigarettes — to anyone under 21 nationwide, closing the gap in states that still allowed sales at 18.
Requires photo ID for any buyer under 30, a stricter check than the federal Tobacco 21 law Congress ultimately enacted, making it harder for older young adults to buy for minors.
Directs the FDA to actively enforce the ban through undercover compliance checks, retailer inspections, and enforcement actions, rather than leaving it to scattered state and local laws.

The bill's findings cite the National Academy of Medicine's projection that raising the sale age to 21 nationally would lead to 223,000 fewer premature deaths, 45,000 fewer lung cancer deaths, and reductions in preterm birth, low birth weight, and sudden infant death syndrome.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco and e-cigarette companies and retailers lose sales to customers aged 18 to 20 — a group the tobacco industry has historically relied on to replace older smokers. Retailers also bear compliance costs and face FDA penalties for violations, and adults aged 18 to 20 lose the ability to buy a legal product.
analysis.who_pays_short: Tobacco companies, e-cigarette makers, and retailers

drawbacks.text: It restricts a legal product for adults aged 18 to 20, taking away the purchasing choice of people old enough to vote, serve in the military, and sign contracts.
The burden of enforcement falls on retailers, including small convenience stores, which face penalties, inspections, and lost sales rather than the manufacturers who make and market the products.

An age ban does not eliminate youth access entirely — it shifts enforcement to compliance checks and can push minors toward older friends or family as sources, which the bill addresses only through the under-30 ID requirement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health case is strong and well documented in the bill itself: tobacco is the leading preventable cause of death, killing more than 480,000 Americans a year and costing about $175 billion in direct medical care annually, and three-quarters of adults — including 7 in 10 smokers — supported the age-21 policy. The costs are real but narrow: restricted choice for 18-to-20-year-olds and lost sales and compliance burdens for retailers. A separate, weaker federal Tobacco 21 law did pass in December 2019 as part of a must-pass spending bill, but it omitted this bill's stricter photo-ID requirement for buyers under 30. On balance, the bill's benefits to public health clearly outweigh its costs; its main flaw is placing enforcement burden on retailers rather than manufacturers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in April 2019 and sat there without a hearing or vote until that Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Brian Schatz introduced the bill on April 30, 2019, with Senators Todd Young, Dick Durbin, and Mitt Romney joining as original cosponsors — a bipartisan group spanning two Democrats and two Republicans.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day it was introduced.
The bill attracted 18 cosponsors — 5 Republicans and 13 Democrats — but the action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action after the referral.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2021, with the bill still in committee, so it never received a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco and e-cigarette companies and retailers kept selling to 18-to-20-year-olds through the life of the bill. Notably, when Congress did raise the national tobacco sale age to 21 in December 2019 via a must-pass spending bill, that law omitted this bill's stricter photo-ID requirement for buyers under 30 — so the industry also avoided that provision.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tobacco and e-cigarette companies and retailers

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start: the bill's four original sponsors split 2 Democrats and 2 Republicans, and its 18 cosponsors split 13 Democrats and 5 Republicans; no senator is recorded as opposing it.

industries.note: An age-21 ban cuts off sales to 18-to-20-year-olds, the critical window when most smokers move from experimenting to daily use, shrinking the pipeline of replacement customers. The bill's own findings state the industry spends billions on marketing aimed at addicting children and continues to challenge tobacco control measures in court.

Vaping products are covered by the bill's tobacco definition, and the bill was written amid a surge in youth vaping — high school e-cigarette use jumped 78% from 2017 to 2018 — so the ban removes the industry's fastest-growing young customer base.

Retailers lose legal sales to 18-to-20-year-old customers and bear the compliance burden: FDA inspections, undercover checks, and civil penalties for violations. They are the enforcement target even though manufacturers profit from the sales.
